doc.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Radio dance bands, first jazz records and the Kenton band in Dublin
summary: Early listening to dance bands and Cab Calloway records, scarce American jazz in Scotland, and seeing Stan Kenton's band in Dublin in 1953 despite the union ban.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What kind of music did you hear as a child?

Well the only kind of music that I vividly remember is dance bands on the radio. You know bands like Henry Hall and Geraldo and those kind of bands. And then when I got a bit older, when I got to be around 14 or 15, I started playing the saxophone when I was 14. And when I was about — first there was no music schools or anything like that so I just had a few lessons locally and then I just had to get on with it myself more or less. I’m still doing that. And the first introduction to jazz actually I had was Cab Calloway’s band. It was a saxophone record. On one side was Chu Berry playing “Ghost of a Chance,” on the other side was “Willow Weep for Me” with Hilton Jefferson. So I’ve spoken to Milt Hinton about that, because he was there. So that’s what I vividly remember. And of © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -3-

course I remembered some things like Benny Goodman “Sing Sing Sing” but it was a very short time. These were 78s and they were very scarce. You know American jazz was very scarce in Scotland. Still is as a matter of fact.
Did you get a chance to hear any of these artists? Did they ever come to Scotland?

No. Not while I was there. Much later they did. I mean they do now, they travel around quite a bit now. And the thing, I spoke to Conte Candoli last night about this because there was a union ban. The British musicians union didn’t allow American musicians to come in to the country to play. So when Conte Candoli came to Ireland with Stan Kenton in 1953, I was working with an English band that also was working in Dublin at the same time. So we got to see the concert. And that band had Lee Konitz and Zoot Sims and Bill Holman and people like that, Conte Candoli, and Frank Rossalino. That was a great band. But that was the first really American jazz orchestra that I ever encountered.
